analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans that cover other prescription drugs to cover prescription contraceptives on equal terms.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 116 cosponsors from both parties, including its Republican sponsor, but was referred to two subcommittees and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar employer health plans and insurance companies from excluding prescription contraceptive drugs, devices, and related outpatient services when the plan covers other prescription drugs and outpatient care. It would also stop insurers from denying enrollment because of a person's use of contraception, stop paying women to accept weaker coverage, and stop rewarding doctors for withholding contraception. The rules would extend to coverage sold to individuals as well as to employer group plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Women of reproductive age with private insurance. The bill's findings note that three-quarters of women of childbearing age rely on private insurance, that women spend 68 percent more than men on out-of-pocket health care largely due to contraception, and that many plans covered no contraceptive method other than sterilization despite covering prescription drugs generally.

how_it_helps.text: Plans covering other outpatient prescription drugs and services could no longer exclude FDA-approved contraceptive drugs, devices, and outpatient contraceptive services.
Insurers could not deny or drop coverage because of a person's actual or potential contraceptive use, and could not pay individuals to accept less protection.
The bill blocks plans from cutting doctors' reimbursement for prescribing contraception or offering incentives to withhold it.
The rules would apply to individual-market policies as well as group plans, and the bill allowed cost-sharing only on the same terms as other covered drugs and services.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers offering group plans, who would bear the cost of an added mandated benefit, presumably passed along in premiums. The bill's own findings argue the cost is small, citing the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program's report of no cost increase after adding contraceptive coverage in 1998.

drawbacks.text: The added benefit would raise premiums for all plan enrollees, including people who never use contraceptives.

The bill contains no conscience or religious exemption, so religiously affiliated employers and insurers would have been required to cover contraception, a dispute that defined later versions of this policy debate.

Plans may still impose deductibles, coinsurance, and prior-authorization rules on contraceptive care so long as they match those for other covered drugs and services, so coverage would not necessarily be free at the point of use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a concrete gap: insurers covered prescription drugs generally but excluded the ones women use to prevent pregnancy, pushing costs onto women and leading to unintended pregnancies. The main costs are modest premium increases spread across enrollees and the unresolved conflict with religious employers. The bill's findings argue contraceptive coverage even saves money by avoiding costlier pregnancies, though that is a sponsor's claim rather than an independent estimate.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, which passed it down to their health-related subcommittees, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2005 without a markup, floor vote, or hearing in the record.

narrative.text: Republican Rep. James Greenwood introduced the bill on July 15, 2003, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee.
Eight days later, each committee referred it to a subcommittee: Health under Energy and Commerce, and Employer-Employee Relations under Education and the Workforce.
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
It attracted 116 cosponsors: 106 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 9 Republicans, including the sponsor.
The bill's findings cite broad public support, saying eight in ten privately insured adults favor contraceptive coverage.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers were spared a federal contraceptive-coverage mandate, and women who would have gained coverage were left paying out of pocket for contraception. Many states later adopted their own contraceptive-coverage mandates instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers; not insured women

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship crossed party lines: 106 Democrats, 9 Republicans, and 1 Independent signed on, with a Republican as lead sponsor, but no committee led by a Republican ever moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have forced insurers to cover prescription contraceptives on the same terms as other drugs, ending the common practice of covering everything except the drugs women use for birth control. Insurers could adjust premiums but could no longer carve this benefit out.

Employers would bear the cost of the added benefit, but the bill's findings cite industry research that not covering contraceptives costs employers 15 to 17 percent more than covering them, through pregnancy-related claims.
A coverage mandate would turn millions of insured women into paying customers for contraceptive drugs and devices that many currently buy out of pocket.
